_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-06) review fixes: 'time to first byte' is renamed 'first bit arrives (one-way delay)' in grey_pager's comment, step 1, terms, the lede and the sim, and a term explains that web tools' time to first byte is a round trip plus server time; the sim's 1 GB transfer is 'a 1 GB file', since the story's backup goes to a storage company in town, not to Halden; limit 2 and the sim add the window-over-round-trip cap (about 23 MB in flight to fill 1 Gbps at 182 ms); new terms (First bit arrives, Time to first byte (web tools), TCP window) and sources (RFC 6349, MDN on time to first byte)
title: The Voice on Line Two

post.author: u/line_two_lena
post.title: I answer phones on a night shift. Since Monday every caller answers a beat too late, and the man on line two sounds farther away each night.

blocks.text: I work nights at Brightwater, a call center in Gannet Bay. When two clinics and a funeral home close, their calls come to us, and six of us agents answer. Our phones are softphones, headsets plugged into laptops. Every call travels as data across the sea to our phone server in Halden, and back across the sea to my headset, though nearly all our callers live right here.

On Monday night the calls changed. I say *Brightwater, how can I help?* and there's a gap, long enough to wonder if anyone's there. Then they start talking just as I say *Hello?*, and we trip over each other all night.

Line two is the worst. Mr. Abernathy calls at 2 AM most nights to ask if his late wife's doctor has phoned back. On Monday his voice came from very far away. On Tuesday, farther. He noticed too: *You sound like you're at the bottom of a well, dear.*
Desmond, our IT guy, ran ping, a tool that sends a tiny message to a machine and times the reply: the round trip. To the phone server it used to say 22 ms. Since Monday:

$ ping halden-phones
64 bytes from halden-phones: icmp_seq=1 time=182 ms
64 bytes from halden-phones: icmp_seq=2 time=182 ms
64 bytes from halden-phones: icmp_seq=3 time=183 ms

Desmond said the line was too thin, and on Wednesday he upgraded our internet from 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps: ten times as many megabits, millions of bits, per second. The nightly backup of call recordings, about a gigabyte, to a storage company in town dropped from 80 seconds to 8. The voices didn't change at all. Ping still says 182.
Then he ran traceroute, which lists every router on the way, each one a hop, with the round trip to each. I kept one time per hop:

$ traceroute halden-phones
 1  office-router            0.3 ms
 2  gannetbay-isp            0.7 ms
 3  landing.gannetbay        1.3 ms
 4  exchange.portcalloway   91.2 ms
 5  landing.halden         181.1 ms
 6  office.halden          181.8 ms
 7  halden-phones          182.1 ms

A landing station is where an undersea cable comes ashore. Hop 3 is ours. Hop 4 is a city I've never been to. Desmond says the direct cable to Halden was cut on Monday, maybe by a ship's anchor, so our calls go the long way round. Repairs take weeks.
Mr. Abernathy called again tonight. He sounded farther away than ever.
Desmond wants to buy an even bigger line. Will that bring the voices back? What would?

diagram.aria: The two routes from Brightwater's call center in Gannet Bay to the phone server in Halden. The direct undersea cable, 2,000 km, is cut. Traffic now goes from Gannet Bay's landing station down to an exchange in Port Calloway and up to Halden's landing station, 18,000 km in all. Ping to the phone server went from 22 ms to 182 ms.

blocks.caption: Desmond drew this on a napkin. The direct cable is cut. Our calls now go 18,000 km by way of Port Calloway, though nearly every caller is on our side of the sea.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Think of the line as a pipe. Bandwidth is how wide it is: how many bits it can carry each second, written Mbps, megabits per second. Latency is how long it is: how long one bit takes to get from one end to the other. Desmond made your pipe ten times wider and left it exactly as long. How long before the first bit arrives, the one-way delay, is set by the length. Throughput, how much actually arrives per second, can never beat the width. A voice packet is tiny. Work out how long it takes to squeeze through 100 Mbps, then compare that with 91 ms.

replies.author: u/line_two_lena
replies.text: A voice packet is about 200 bytes, so 1,600 bits. At 100 million bits a second that's 0.016 ms. Then 91 ms of travelling. The width was never the problem, was it?

comments.author: u/bits_not_bytes
comments.text: For Desmond: Mbps is mega*bits* per second. Download windows show MB/s, mega*bytes*. A byte is 8 bits, so 1 Gbps (a thousand Mbps) tops out at 125 MB/s, before overhead. Your 1 GB backup at 1 Gbps: 8 billion bits at a billion a second, 8 seconds. That part checks out.

comments.author: u/packet_ghost
comments.text: Watch for packet loss on the long route too. Calls use UDP, so a lost voice packet is just gone and a word gets clipped. The backup uses TCP, which resends what's lost and slows down when it sees loss, and every resend waits at least one round trip. The longer the pipe, the more each loss costs.

reply.prompt: Desmond can spend the budget once. What should Brightwater do so the calls sound normal again? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Upgrade again, from 1 Gbps to 10 Gbps. If ten times wider didn't do it, a hundred times wider will.
options.part2: Desmond signed for 10 Gbps. The backup now finishes before I can stand up. Ping: 182 ms. At 2 AM Mr. Abernathy still sounded like he was calling from the bottom of a well.
options.senior: Bandwidth is width. The delay is the length of the route, and no amount of width makes it shorter. A voice packet already squeezes through 100 Mbps in a sliver of a millisecond.

options.text: Switch the phones to a setting that squeezes each call into less data, so every call uses a quarter of the bandwidth.
options.part2: Desmond switched every phone to the squeezed setting. Each call used a quarter of the bandwidth. Voices went thin and crackly, like an old radio, and the gap before every answer stayed exactly the same length.
options.senior: Squeezing saves bandwidth, but the line was never full. Smaller packets still take 91 ms to cross the sea, twice. Squeezing and unsqueezing the sound can even add a few milliseconds of its own.

options.text: Pay the provider for a premium route over another cable that reaches Halden by a shorter path, at three times the price.
options.verdict: Shorter, but you still cross the sea
options.part2: The premium route cut ping to Halden to 64 ms. Calls felt almost normal, with a slight lag you stopped noticing after an hour. The bill tripled. When the direct cable was repaired in March, we were still paying for the premium route, because nobody remembered to cancel it.
options.senior: A shorter route attacks the real problem, length, and sometimes it's the right call. But Brightwater is paying to send local calls across the sea and back at all. Moving the call handling close to the callers removes the trip instead of shortening it.

options.text: Shorten the trip: until the cable is fixed, run Gannet Bay's calls through a phone server on this side of the sea, close to both the callers and the agents, and keep pinging Halden to see when the direct route is back.
options.part2: Desmond set up a small phone server in a data center twenty minutes from the office and moved our calls onto it on Thursday night. Ping to it: 2 ms. At 2 AM line two rang. *Brightwater, how can I help?* "Hello, dear," said Mr. Abernathy, right on time and close as the next room. He asked if his wife's doctor had called. I said not yet. He said, "She says you sound much better tonight."
options.senior: When small things arrive late, the fix is distance, not width. Keep local traffic local, measure the round trip before and after, and keep the far server for when the path is healthy again.

sim.title: Two call centers and a pipe
sim.lede: This is the line from Brightwater in Gannet Bay to the phone server in Halden, drawn as a pipe. Drag the distance to make it longer and the bandwidth to make it wider. Then send a 1 KB message or a 1 GB file and compare when the first bit arrives (the one-way delay), the total time and the throughput. Run traceroute to see the round trip to each hop. The pipe here is perfect: no other traffic, no packet loss and none of TCP's limits.
sim.tryThis: Try this: send the 1 KB message at 2,000 km, then make the pipe ten times wider and send it again. Now drag the distance to 18,000 km, the long way round, and send it once more. Then send a 1 GB file at 100 Mbps and at 1 Gbps. Run traceroute at both distances and find the hop where the time jumps.

explain.oneLine: The line didn't get thinner. It got longer. The direct cable was cut, calls took an 18,000 km detour, and every voice crossed it twice. Making a pipe wider can't make it shorter.

steps.title: Length and width are different things.
steps.text: Picture the line as a pipe. Bandwidth is its width: how many bits it can carry each second. Latency is its length: how long one bit takes to get from one end to the other. Throughput is what you actually get, how much arrives per second over a whole transfer, and it's never more than the width. A message's total time is roughly the latency plus its size divided by the bandwidth. The first bit can't arrive sooner than the latency, however wide the pipe is. That first arrival, the moment the first bit gets there, is the one-way delay.

steps.title: Light is fast, but the planet is big.
steps.text: Light in optical fiber covers roughly 200 km every millisecond. The direct cable to Halden is about 2,000 km, so 10 ms each way, and the routers along the way add a little: ping said 22 ms for the round trip. The detour through Port Calloway is about 18,000 km, 90 ms each way, and ping says 182. And a call crosses twice, caller to Halden and Halden to the agent, so a voice now takes about 182 ms to arrive. When the agent finishes a sentence, the caller hears the end of it 182 ms later, and the reply needs another 182 ms to come back: over a third of a second of extra silence every time someone stops talking.

steps.title: Why the upgrade sped up the backup and nothing else.
steps.text: A 1 KB message is 8,000 bits. Through 100 Mbps it takes 0.08 ms to push in, and through 1 Gbps, 0.008 ms. Either way it then spends about 91 ms crossing the sea. A voice packet is smaller still. The backup is the opposite: 1 GB is 8,000,000,000 bits, 80 seconds through 100 Mbps and 8 seconds through 1 Gbps, and its trip across town takes under a millisecond. Small messages are latency-bound. Big transfers are bandwidth-bound. Mind the units too: line speeds count bits (Mbps), and download windows show bytes (MB/s). 8 bits make a byte, so 1 Gbps is at most 125 MB/s.

steps.title: ping and traceroute measure the length.
steps.text: ping sends an ICMP echo request, a tiny control message, and times the echo reply: one round trip, once a second by default, with a summary of packets lost and the minimum, average and maximum times. traceroute finds the hops. Every packet carries a time to live, a hop counter that each router lowers by one. When it reaches zero, that router drops the packet and sends back a *time exceeded* message. traceroute sends probes with a time to live of 1, then 2, then 3, three probes each, so each router on the path answers in turn, and a * means a probe got no answer. The jump from 1.3 ms at hop 3 to 91.2 ms at hop 4 is the long cable. This time to live counts hops. It isn't the DNS timer from the radio station's case.

steps.title: Packet loss hurts more on a long pipe.
steps.text: Calls use UDP, so a lost voice packet is simply gone and a word gets clipped. The backup uses TCP, which resends what's lost, and TCP's congestion rules (RFC 5681) also make the sender cut its sending rate when it detects loss. Each resend waits at least a round trip, so the same loss costs more at 182 ms than at 22 ms. Long pipes have one more catch: a TCP connection can only have so much data in flight before an acknowledgment comes back, and on a path that is both wide and long, RFC 7323 warns, that limit can hold throughput below the bandwidth.

diagram.aria: Total transfer time is latency plus size divided by bandwidth. Latency is the pipe's length: over the 18,000 km route it is 91 ms one way at any width. Size divided by bandwidth is the pipe's width: a 1 GB file at 1 Gbps takes 8 seconds, and ten times the width makes it ten times faster. A 1 KB message spends almost all its time on latency: 91 ms plus 0.008 ms. A 1 GB file spends almost all its time on bandwidth: 0.09 seconds plus 8 seconds.

explain.caption: Every transfer pays both parts. Over the 18,000 km detour at 1 Gbps, a 1 KB message spends 91 ms travelling and 0.008 ms squeezing through; a 1 GB file spends 0.09 s travelling and 8 s squeezing through. Widening the pipe only shrinks the right-hand part.

fix.title: The fix: shorten the trip, then keep measuring it
fix.text: Until the cable is repaired, handle Gannet Bay's calls on a phone server close to Gannet Bay, in a nearby data center, so neither leg of a call crosses the sea. Keep Halden as the backup and move calls back when ping shows the direct route is healthy again. Keep the 1 Gbps line if the backups and other big transfers need it; it just isn't a cure for distance. Then watch the length, not only the width: ping the phone server every minute and raise an alert when the round trip jumps, and run traceroute when it does, so you can see which hop got longer.

limits: You can't beat the speed of light. If the people on a call really are far apart, the delay is real. You can only avoid adding to it, for example by not sending local calls the long way round.

The sim treats the pipe as perfect. Real transfers also lose time to TCP's handshake and its slow start, and one TCP connection can never go faster than its window, the data it may have in flight, divided by the round trip. Filling 1 Gbps over the detour's 182 ms round trip needs a window of about 23 MB; with a smaller one, a 1 GB file sent the long way takes longer than the sim's 8 seconds.
ping and traceroute need ICMP answers, and many firewalls drop them. A silent ping or a row of * in traceroute can mean a machine that ignores probes, not a broken path.

head: What you pay for
Helps
Doesn't help
rows: Delay on small messages like voice, clicks and pings.
Delay on everything that crosses it.
Costs more, and it's still as long as the shortest cable.
Delay mostly disappears for nearby users.
A second system to run, and users far from it get nothing.

explain.seniorTake: Ask what kind of slow it is. If small things arrive late, it's latency: shorten the path or move the work closer. If big things take long, it's bandwidth or throughput: widen the pipe or send less. ping and traceroute tell you which before you spend anything.

realWorld.title: Red Sea, February 24, 2024
realWorld.text: Cloudflare's summary of internet disruptions for the first quarter of 2024 reports that on February 24 three submarine cables running through the Red Sea were damaged: Seacom/Tata, AAE-1 and EIG. It says the cables are believed to have been cut by the anchor of the Rubymar, a cargo ship damaged by a missile on February 18. The damage reportedly affected countries in East Africa, including Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda and Mozambique, yet Cloudflare Radar observed no loss of traffic across those countries.

realWorld.title: Red Sea again, September 2025
realWorld.text: Kentik's Doug Madory wrote up a new set of Red Sea cable breaks in September 2025. Public reports named SMW-4 and IMEWE as impacted. In the cloud measurements Kentik publishes, AWS's region in Bahrain saw latency spikes to other cloud regions in the Gulf and to AWS locations outside the region, and Google Cloud's Doha region saw a jump in latency to regions in the Gulf, Europe and South Asia. For the affected countries, he described the loss of transit as subtle, mostly losing some of their routes out. And he noted that even the biggest cloud companies rely on the same submarine cables as everyone else.

realWorld.title: What ping and traceroute actually do
realWorld.text: The traceroute manual says it uses the IP protocol's time to live field to get an ICMP TIME_EXCEEDED reply from each gateway on the way to the host, sending three probes at each time to live by default, up to 30 hops, and printing * when a probe gets no answer in time. The ping manual says it sends ICMP ECHO_REQUEST packets to get an ECHO_RESPONSE, waits one second between packets by default, and reports packet loss and round-trip times.

asked: What's the difference between latency and bandwidth?
Users far away say the app feels slow. How do you find out why, and what do you do about it?
interview.answer: Latency is how long one thing takes to get there, set mostly by distance and the hops in between. Bandwidth is how much can flow per second, and throughput is what you actually get. Total time is roughly latency plus size divided by bandwidth, so small requests are latency-bound and big transfers are bandwidth-bound. To diagnose, measure round trips with ping, the path with traceroute, and look for a jump at one hop; then check whether the complaint is small things being slow or big things being slow. For latency: serve users from closer (more regions, a CDN), cut sequential round trips (batch requests, reuse connections), and avoid detours. More bandwidth only fixes the second kind of slow.

terms.def: An office of people who answer phone calls for other businesses, often at night when those businesses are closed.
A person who answers calls at a call center.
A phone that's really a program on a computer, with a headset plugged in. Its calls travel as packets of data over the internet.
The program that connects calls: it takes the caller's voice packets and passes them to an agent's softphone, and back the other way.
How much data a link can carry each second: the width of the pipe. Written in bits per second, like 100 Mbps.
How long data takes to get from one end to the other: the length of the pipe. Mostly set by distance and the hops in between.
How much data actually arrives per second over a whole transfer. Never more than the bandwidth, and often much less.
The moment the first bit of a message reaches the far end: the one-way delay. Set by latency, not bandwidth. The sim shows it in milliseconds.
What browsers and web tools call the time from sending a request to the first byte of the reply: at least a full round trip plus the server's own time. Not the one-way delay.
The time for a message to reach the far end and for a reply to come back. Written RTT. It's what ping measures.
The time for data to travel in one direction: about half the round trip.
How long it takes to push a whole message into the link: its size in bits divided by the bandwidth. The width part of the total.
How long a signal takes to travel the length of the link. Light in fiber covers about 200 km per millisecond. The length part of the total.
Slow mostly because of distance: small messages, clicks and voice. More bandwidth barely helps.
Slow mostly because of size: big downloads, backups and video. More bandwidth helps a lot.
The smallest unit of data: a single 0 or 1. Line speeds are counted in bits.
8 bits make a byte. Line speeds use bits (Mbps), and file sizes and download windows use bytes (MB, MB/s). Divide Mbps by 8 to get MB/s.
Megabits per second: a million bits each second. 100 Mbps is at most 12.5 megabytes per second.
Gigabits per second: a billion bits each second, or 1,000 Mbps. 1 Gbps is at most 125 MB per second.
Megabytes per second: a million bytes each second. Download windows usually show this.
A megabyte is a million bytes. A gigabyte is a billion bytes, or 1,000 MB. The nightly backup is about 1 GB.
A copy of data kept somewhere else, so it survives if the original is lost. Brightwater copies its call recordings every night.
A tool that sends a small message to a machine and times the reply, usually once a second, then reports the round trips and any packets lost.
A tool that lists the routers between you and a machine, with the round-trip time to each one.
One router along a path. Each hop adds a little delay; a long cable between two hops adds a lot.
Internet Control Message Protocol: small control messages machines send each other, like ping's echo request and echo reply, or time exceeded.
A hop counter in every packet. Each router lowers it by one; at zero the packet is dropped and the router may send back time exceeded. Not DNS's TTL.
The ICMP message a router sends back when a packet's time to live runs out there. traceroute uses it to find each hop.
A fiber cable laid along the sea floor between countries. Most traffic between continents travels through them.
The building where an undersea cable comes ashore and joins the network on land.
The path packets take from one machine to another, hop by hop. When a cable breaks, routers pick another route, often a longer one.
More traffic than a link can carry, so routers queue packets or drop them. TCP slows down when it sees loss, assuming congestion.
Data that has been sent but not yet acknowledged. TCP limits how much can be in flight, so on a long pipe it may wait instead of filling it.
How much data one TCP connection may have in flight before an acknowledgment comes back. Its speed can never beat the window divided by the round trip.
RFC 7323's name for a path with both high bandwidth and long delay, where one TCP connection can struggle to use the whole width.
Paid access to the rest of the internet that one network buys from a bigger one. Losing some transit means fewer routes out.
Cloudflare's public website of internet traffic data, which shows outages and disruptions around the world.
A company that sells network monitoring and publishes analysis of internet events, including cloud latency measurements.
Content delivery network: servers in many cities that keep copies of a site's files close to users, so each request travels a shorter distance.
An AWS service whose Infrastructure Performance page shows round-trip latency between AWS Regions and Availability Zones, measured by AWS's own probes.

atWork: Pick two places your team runs things, such as two AWS Regions or two Availability Zones, and open the Infrastructure Performance page in AWS Network Manager with read access. It shows the round-trip latency between them, measured by AWS's own probes and reported as the median of each five-minute window. Write the number down. Then, from a machine you can already log in to, ping a server in the far location and run traceroute to it, and compare. If ping gets no answer, check the target's security group: AWS's docs say pinging an instance needs an inbound ICMP echo request rule. Finally, find one request in your system that crosses that distance more than once, and ask whether it needs to.

recall.prompt: Users in Singapore say your app, which runs only in a data center in Virginia, feels sluggish: every click takes a beat. Your manager wants to double the servers' bandwidth. What do you check, and what do you suggest instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Measure the latency with ping or traceroute
More bandwidth won't speed up small requests
Serve them from closer: a nearer region or a CDN
Cut the number of round trips

recall.model: Measure first: ping and traceroute from Singapore to Virginia will show a round trip of very roughly a couple of hundred milliseconds, set by distance. Each click is a small request, so it's latency-bound, and doubling the bandwidth won't change it. Suggest serving Singapore from closer, such as an Asian region or a CDN for the files that don't change, and cutting how many round trips each click needs, by batching requests and reusing connections.

recall.prompt: A 1 KB message crosses an 18,000 km fiber route. The link is upgraded from 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps. Roughly what happens to its delivery time?
options: It drops to about a tenth
It barely changes: about 91 ms either way
recall.why: Pushing 8,000 bits into the link takes 0.08 ms at 100 Mbps and 0.008 ms at 1 Gbps. The 91 ms of travelling along 18,000 km of fiber doesn't change at all.

recall.prompt: Your connection is sold as 1 Gbps. What's the fastest a download window could ever show?
recall.why: Gbps counts bits; download windows count bytes. 8 bits make a byte, so a billion bits a second is at most 125 million bytes a second, and a little less after overhead.

recall.prompt: traceroute shows 1.3 ms at hop 3 and 91.2 ms at hop 4. What does that tell you?
options: There's a long stretch of path between hops 3 and 4, most likely a long cable
Packets are being lost at hop 4
recall.why: Each line is the round trip to that hop. A jump of about 90 ms between two neighbours means roughly 9,000 km of fiber between them: the long way round.

recall.prompt: Explain to Desmond, in plain words, why the 1 GB backup got ten times faster but the voices didn't change at all.

keyIdeas.idea: Every transfer pays two parts: the trip and the squeeze
Voice packets are tiny, so they're all trip: latency
The backup is huge, so it's all squeeze: bandwidth

recall.model: Everything you send pays for two things: the trip along the pipe, which depends on its length, and squeezing all of it through, which depends on its width. A voice packet is tiny, so it squeezes through in a sliver of a millisecond and then spends 91 ms travelling: all trip. The backup is a gigabyte, so the trip across town is nothing and squeezing 8 billion bits through takes 80 seconds at 100 Mbps: all squeeze. Ten times the width made the squeeze ten times shorter and left the trip exactly as long.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 6 months later. The cable's fixed, and Brightwater is opening a second night shift in Port Calloway, about 9,000 km from Halden. Desmond's plan: send Port Calloway's calls through the Halden phone server like everyone else's, and buy Port Calloway a 10 Gbps line "so the calls are crisp."
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Will Port Calloway's calls sound right? What should Desmond do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: 9,000 km is about 45 ms each way, and each call crosses it twice
Put a phone server near Port Calloway
Measure with ping and traceroute before going live

coldCase.model: No. Port Calloway's callers and agents are both about 9,000 km of fiber from Halden: roughly 45 ms each way, plus the routers. Every call would cross that twice, caller to Halden and Halden to agent, so about 90 ms before a voice arrives and nearly 200 ms of extra silence every time someone stops talking: Monday night all over again. 10 Gbps changes none of that, because a voice packet already squeezes through 100 Mbps in a sliver of a millisecond. Run Port Calloway's calls on a phone server near Port Calloway, keep Halden as the backup, and ping and traceroute both before going live.

next: Next: an abandoned server closet, a black screen, and someone who logs in at 3:14 every night.

Kentik blog: Subsea Cables Parted in Red Sea Again, by Doug Madory (September 9, 2025)
traceroute(8) manual, via man7.org (time to live, ICMP TIME_EXCEEDED, three probes per hop, 30 hops by default, * for no answer)
ping(8) manual, iputils, via man7.org (ICMP ECHO_REQUEST and ECHO_RESPONSE, one second between packets by default, loss and round-trip statistics)
RFC 7323: TCP Extensions for High Performance (IETF, September 2014): long, fat networks and the bandwidth times delay product
RFC 5681: TCP Congestion Control (IETF, September 2009): what a sender must do when it detects loss
AWS Network Manager: How Infrastructure Performance works (round-trip latency between Regions and Availability Zones, median of each five-minute interval)
Amazon EC2 User Guide: Security group rules for different use cases (rules for ping and ICMP)
RFC 6349: Framework for TCP Throughput Testing (IETF, August 2011): BDP = RTT x bottleneck bandwidth, minimum TCP receive window = BDP / 8, TCP throughput = window x 8 / RTT
MDN Web Docs glossary: Time to First Byte (from the browser's request to the first byte of the response, including DNS lookup and the TCP and TLS handshakes)
